scope: Explicitly dated, recoverable concrete record findings, supported factual corrections, reviewed relationship assessments and selected working family connections. Dates and explicit date ranges are research retrieval, supplied-record review, original-reading or explicitly dated relationship-review dates stated in maintained evidence, not historical event dates or file modification. Entries based on earlier checked readings identify that reuse and do not imply fresh original inspection. Selected uncertain links retain their individual probabilities, dependencies, alternatives and prior assessment; record-defined kinship is distinguished from adult identity. Undated conclusions, pure confirmations, unselected speculative parent rankings, negative searches and routine profile/build activity are excluded. This is a recoverable dated history, not an exhaustive account of all past research.

findings.finding: The Larne session minutes naming John Glasgow, sen., Robert Glasgow and James Glasgow belong to 1700 and 1701, not 1699 and 1700. John and Robert were stipend bondsmen for Kilwaughter and the South Side on 17 May 1700; James was made overseer for Kilwaughter probably on Thursday 29 May 1701.
findings.qualification: Porter prints the minutes under 1699 and 1700 from a manuscript copy of the session record. He corrects the stipend run to 1700 himself and the weekdays confirm it; the 1701 date for James is an inference from the weekdays. The minutes state no relationship between the three men. No live WikiTree change.

sources.title: Porter, Congregational Memoirs: Larne and Kilwaughter, The Christian Unitarian 2 (1863), pp. 410-414
The same, The Christian Unitarian 3 (1864), pp. 16-19

findings.finding: The Robert Glasgow marked “turned out” on the Larne session list of 1721-1769 and the Robert Glasgow of the discipline minute of 17 May 1747 are one man, probably Robert Glasgow of Kilwaughter (Glasgow-1143) and not the Robert of 1700-01.
findings.qualification: Porter’s footnote ties the list note to the 1747 minute. The identification rests on age (the older Robert would have been in his late sixties or more) and Kilwaughter residence; no record states it, and a third Robert cannot be excluded. No live WikiTree change.

findings.finding: William Agnew’s lease of Ballykeel to Robert Glasgow is dated 13 February 1738 Old Style (1739 by modern reckoning) and was registered on 22 May 1742. Its three lives are Robert, “Jas Glasgow Junr” and Rachel “otherwise Wilson Wife to the sd Robt Glasgow”; it names no second James and gives Robert no residence.
findings.qualification: Read on the saved register images of memorial 74015 by two readers. “Junior” points to an older namesake and states no relationship. No live WikiTree change.

findings.finding: Robert Glasgow of Kilwaughter was alive on 20 December 1764, when he leased half of Ballykeel to Hugh Shannon, and probably in April 1772. “About 1772” is a last sighting, not a death estimate, and “about 1710” would make him a groom of 19; about 1708 or earlier fits the records.
findings.qualification: No record gives his age or his death. The 1772 declaration’s date and Kilwaughter heading are known only second-hand. The WikiTree dates are queued for review, not changed.

findings.finding: Rachel Wilson’s birth “about 1680” has no source and would make her 51, 53 and 58 at the baptisms of her children in 1731, 1733 and 1738. The records allow about 1690 to 1712.
findings.qualification: An estimate: it assumes a bride of at least about 17 in November 1729 and a mother of no more than about 48 in November 1738. The marriage and baptisms are known from a derivative register chronology. The WikiTree date is queued for review, not changed.

findings.finding: The ruling elder James Glasgow of the General Synod rolls is printed beside William Taylor of Drumaul in 1698 and 1703 and beside James Scott of Duneane in 1705; Larne’s own elder in 1703 was James Caldwell. He is probably not James Glasgow of Kilwaughter.

findings.finding: Four original-checked Belfast News-Letter passages from 1840 name Rev. Adam Glasgow: as officiant at a James and Margaret Small marriage, as opening a Townsend-street Presbyterian soirée, among speakers at the Belfast Town Mission annual meeting, and among two Synod ministers accepted for India mission service with James Carr. The Synod report says Kathiawar or Guzerat was selected and gives a planned 4 August departure overland to Bombay.
findings.qualification: The notices give no middle name or unique identifier; the ministerial context is compatible with, but does not uniquely identify, Glasgow-1781. “Wednesday evening last” for the Town Mission meeting is retained as printed. The August journey is planned, not proof of departure. The separate Synod passage names James Carr, not James Glasgow, and establishes no kinship. The 1842 Nancy marriage notice is not included here because the same fact was already documented; it is added only as primary-source corroboration.

findings.finding: Original-checked Belfast News-Letter passages name James Glasgow as a Belfast College essay award recipient in 1829; Rev. James Glasgow of Castledawson at a Bellaghy ordination in 1836 and among missionaries set apart for India in 1840; a source of a letter reported in 1841; the signer of a Rajkote letter dated 14 August 1841; and the first Moderator of the first Indian Presbytery in 1842.
findings.qualification: The 1829 student is only a possible match to Glasgow-1780. The Castledawson and missionary passages are probable matches within the established career sequence, but these notices do not give James’s middle name. The 1836 ordination date (15 March) is inferred from “15th ult.”; the issue date is 5 April. The 1841 May report gives no letter date; the October letter is dated 14 August. The separate Adam Glasgow passages on the 1840 and 1842 issues do not establish kinship. “Brother missionary” describes colleague Alexander Kerr, not a biological brother. No family certainty changes.

daniel-glasco.assessment: Daniel Glasco/Glascow, Norfolk planter, and his wife Mary conveyed 100 acres from Henry Slade’s 330-acre patent to Richard Linton. The upper endorsement expressly says Daniel came into court and acknowledged the act on 3 September 1729, proving him alive then. Daneill Glasco and Richard Linton also witnessed Richard Johnson’s will dated 26 February 1729/30; McIntosh’s abstract is printed page 122. Glasgow-3322, Mary Gamon’s husband in 1693, remains compatible, but the two estates have no proved continuous title chain.

mary.assessment: Mary is expressly Daniel Glasco’s wife in the 1729 deed. Gammon-934 remains compatible with the 1693 John Gamon will’s daughter Mary, wife of Daniel Glasco. Her guessed 1699 death and inconsistent imported spouse field are unsupported and do not exclude her. The 1693 record proves that earlier Mary’s father, but no record yet proves that the 1729 wife is the same woman. Keep the candidate and the lifetime identity qualification together.

richard-linton.assessment: Richard Linton purchased the 1729 land and witnessed Richard Johnson’s will dated 26 February 1729/30 with Daneill Glasco. Linton-898 remains compatible: its estimated 1680 birth, missing death and sparse Virginia family context supply no concrete conflict. Linton-931 also remains a weaker compatible candidate because its 1722 birth is GEDCOM-derived. Linton-494 has cited Lancaster death/probate in 1665, a concrete conflict with the 1729 transaction. Keep the candidate; cite McIntosh’s printed page 122 and do not infer survival to probate.

mary-thomson.assessment: Mary Thomson, age 37, married William Sneddon on 9 November 1860; the fresh index names her parents Robert Thomson and Mary Glasgon Thomson. Thomson-3009 remains a disputed candidate because its estimated 1826 birth and James/Helen GEDCOM parents are unsupported. Thomson-13010 has record-based Andrew Thomson/Elizabeth Waddell parents and a distinct Abercrombie household, a concrete conflict with the indexed bride. Index parentage is not an existing-profile father upgrade, and the restricted original remains uninspected.

william-sneddon.assessment: The fresh 1860 index identifies William Sneddon, age 45, widower and collier, with parents Robert Sneddon and Mary Gray Sneddon. Sneddon-710 remains a candidate: its Pencaitland coal-mining household and wife Mary Wilson allow a later widowed marriage. However, age 30 in 1841 normally means 30–34, implying birth about 1806–1811 rather than the 1860 estimate of 1815. This is a material discrepancy. No record joins the indexed parents to Sneddon-710. Obtain the 1851/1861 census, first wife’s death and accessible original; do not attach Sneddon-92, whose recorded wife was Mary Snaddon, daughter of Richard Snaddon and Mary Hoggan.

james-glasgow.assessment: The live biographies identify two distinct adult Larne men: James Glasgow-1509, ropemaker (1737–1802), and James Glasgow-3991, probable tanner (about 1748–1812). Both survived until the 1779 lease. The separate 1768 messuage names a ropemaker party and a farmer witness, whose roles require separate comparison. Glasgow-1509 is the leading compatible party. No source names the farmer witness's relatives or identifies the 1779 lessee. The 1832 renewal does not establish Anne or Jane as James’s daughters. Keep the 1768 ropemaker party, farmer witness and 1779 lessee roles separate. Jane, wife of Glasgow-3991, died in 1820 and cannot be the 1832 lessee.

anne-glasgow.assessment: Ann Glasgow-3992, born about 1768, died on 25 May 1832 at Larne and was alive on the 25 February 1832 renewal date. Her armorial inscription names father James and mother Jane, fitting the local generation, but does not identify this lease. Ann and Anne are compatible name forms. The 1832 renewal does not establish Anne or Jane as James’s daughters. Keep the 1768 ropemaker party, farmer witness and 1779 lessee roles separate. Jane, wife of Glasgow-3991, died in 1820 and cannot be the 1832 lessee.

jane-glasgow.assessment: Jane Glasgow-4013 is the strongest locality candidate: her live biography describes Larne probate entries in 1844–1846 and birth before 1826, rather than an actual 1826 birth. Jane Glasgow-3929, born 5 October 1802 and later wife of John Gray, is also chronologically compatible. A different husband and missing lease connection do not exclude her. The 1832 renewal does not establish Anne or Jane as James’s daughters. Keep the 1768 ropemaker party, farmer witness and 1779 lessee roles separate. Jane, wife of Glasgow-3991, died in 1820 and cannot be the 1832 lessee.

thomas-ross.assessment: The original 1901 Gortereghy return describes Thomas Ross, 34, as farmer and flax miller, with Scotland-born wife Mary Jane and children. This strongly supports the 1912 mill-owner occurrence. The 1911 household reports 24 years of marriage. Ross-13124 remains compatible, with differing reported census ages. Ross-29596 has severe chronology tension if his cited 1874 birth is correct: he would be about 12 at marriage and 11 when Jeannie was born. The birth image returned HTTP 403, so this remains a conditional conflict rather than a fresh original-based exclusion. Ross-25888 has a separate Gransha/Ann Jane family; Ross-29600 is Robert T Ross, who died in 1909.

findings.finding: The published headstone transcription for Rasharkin Second Presbyterian Church records a memorial erected by Alexander Elder of Gortrickey to his father Robert Elder, his mother Jane, and his sisters and brothers. It also records Alexander Elder's death on 5 January 1943.
findings.qualification: This is a new direct memorial transcription for the catalogue's parentage study, not a Glasgow record and not proof that the Elder family was related to Alexander Glasgow. Its value is locality context: Gortrickey/Gortereghy is the townland where the Glasgow family appears in the 1837–1838 Rasharkin Presbyterian baptism entries. The memorial supplies a named Elder household for future comparison with the later Robert Elder who occupied Alexander Glasgow's former Lisnagaver lot; identity between those Elder references remains unproved.

robert-elder-father.assessment: Elder-7144 remains compatible for the living 1901 father of Alex/Robert/Eliza/Margaretta; its 1827 birth is tree-derived and differs from reported age 65, so retain uncertainty. Elder-7251 represents Mary Glasgow’s separate Gortahar family: she is a widow there in 1901 while the Gortereghy Robert is alive. Do not exclude Elder-7251 globally from Sarah’s 1893 father clause merely because a father can be deceased at marriage. Sarah and Isaac’s father occurrences remain unproved bridges to the 1901 family. The original 1881 Jane birth proves Robert/Jane Calderwood as a parental couple, not the mother identity of all later siblings.

alexander-elder.assessment: The original 1901 Alex is explicitly Robert’s son; the 1911 return names brother Robert and sister Margaret. Together with the 1908 Alexander/Mary Anderson marriage extract, these support one sibling family. Retain the actual age differences. Use the same qualified Elder-7144 father hypothesis for Alexander and proved siblings; mother Jane on the memorial is separately evidenced, while Jane Calderwood remains a comparison. No matching Alexander profile was established in full same-name and father-filtered searches.

david-mathy.assessment: David Mathy and Mergaret Androsoune, expressly his spouse, bought a barn at Powdrait, Glasgow, on 3 February 1550/51. David Mathy and Robert Glesgw were expressly fellow burgesses witnessing a sasine on 10 May 1554; David also witnessed an act on 4 July 1554. The name and city make the purchaser and witness probably the same man, but the later acts do not repeat the spouse. No kinship with Robert is stated. David Matthew-330 is a weak compatible variant candidate: its only 1701 death assertion is GEDCOM-derived, so it cannot be excluded. The complete sourced draft remains on HOLD against that candidate, with purchaser/witness identity qualified.

findings.finding: Agnes Glasgow, wife of John Logan at Stevenston, is selected as an uncertain working daughter of James Glasgow younger of Corsankell.
findings.qualification: No record names Agnes’s father. Parish, generation and the existing family comparisons support only a low-confidence choice. The 1601 entry is a land-record registration, not a marriage date or an age statement; Agnes may already have been married for many years. As an illustration only, a married woman aged about 20–35 in 1601 would have been born about 1566–1581, making James younger about 26–41 and James elder about 51–66 at her birth. These are comparison assumptions, not birth estimates or exclusions. James elder remains an alternative father if Agnes was older. Edward Glasgow-1557 or another local Glasgow remains an alternative, especially if the unproved sisterhood with Jonet Glasgow-1494 is established. Edward’s own approximate 1570 birth makes that father generation less comfortable for a woman already married in 1601, but the estimate is not a hard conflict. No mother or proved siblinghood. The public c.1610 birth estimate is superseded by unknown birth and a conditional before-1601 boundary from the probable sasine identity. No new original inspection or certainty upgrade.

findings.finding: The Saltcoats sailor and his documented daughters are restored as one family, with the earlier Corsankell John selected as his uncertain working father.
findings.qualification: No source names the sailor’s parents or age. His former c.1600 birth was an unsupported creation estimate; it is not replaced by an invented older birth to fit this hypothesis. If a birth near 1600 is eventually established, the earlier John would have been an older father, and a grandson or more distant collateral placement could be more natural. Same given name is weak support and does not distinguish this candidate securely from Glasgow-3921 (James younger), another member of the local family, or an unrecorded father. The sailor could belong elsewhere in that family or to another branch. The 1559–60 Kilwinning attribution to the Corsankell John is itself probable, although the 1571 Corsankell family is directly recorded. The same-person alternative is less economical: an adult in 1559 would have been about 95 or older at the sailor’s death in 1636, assuming adulthood at eighteen. That is an illustrative age comparison, not a proved exclusion. The father-versus-grandfather degree remains open. No mother is assigned to the sailor or to his daughters; Agnes Wilson’s joint tenancy does not make her his mother, and Isobell Gray’s widowhood does not prove her maternity. The girls’ already-proved father links remain proved. No identity merge, new original inspection, live WikiTree save or confidence upgrade is made. The missing page was a catalogue omission; the two daughter links were already confident on 28 September.

findings.finding: The Whitecastle James was reported imprisoned in July 1672, not fined in 1670. The printed decree and named Biggar-area neighbours support a probable Libberton setting. A conditional uncertain father in the existing Quothquan family is now selected through the possible Lindsaylands identity.
findings.qualification: The printed decree in Robert Wodrow’s 1721 History, volume I, appendix no. XLVII, pp.133–134, is dated 27 July 1672 in both its heading and Latin opening. It names “James Glasgow in Whitecastle” among people imprisoned for refusing the oath. The monetary fines there belong to Mr James Duncan and the Countess of Wigtoun, not to James Glasgow. William Crookshank’s 1751 summary, volume I p.285, places the same named group under 24 July 1672; preserve that day discrepancy and prefer the printed decree’s 27 July for this source account. Neither source supports the old 1670 date. The two books recount the same proceeding and are not independent evidence of two imprisonments. The surrounding Biggar/Boghall group names men in Biggar, Carwood, Edmonstoun, Worslyd and Carstairs. This favours the Whitecastle in Libberton parish over a location guessed merely from general Covenanter activity. J. L. Davidson’s published article title locates West Whitecastle Farm in Libberton, Lanarkshire (Proceedings of the Society of Antiquaries of Scotland 108, p.383; title checked in the journal’s search-indexed contents, full article not inspected). This supports the Libberton place identification, in the same parish setting as Quothquan and near Biggar’s Lindsaylands; it does not identify a seventeenth-century occupier. This is a probable interpretation of James’s residence, not a parish supplied literally by the decree. White Castle in Garvald and Bara, East Lothian, is a real alternative place. The decree also deals with a Perthshire group; document order alone does not put every accused person in Clydesdale. There are two dependent gaps: Whitecastle James is not proved to be the Lindsaylands weaver, and John’s paternity of James-3332 is itself unproved. John’s 1685 Quothquan testament names his widow but no child; the absence of James, if dead by 1680, would not exclude this model. James-3332’s possible identity with the 1624 weaver would invalidate this particular later-life route, because the 1624 decedent cannot be the man present in 1672. James-1150, the Edinburgh weaver, remains an alternative adult identification for the later weaver rather than being excluded from an unsupported birth estimate; another local James or a different kinship degree remains possible. The old Marion-baptism role error supplies no positive parentage for James-1376, and the Duffe household James-2682 is not merged. The 1738 Edinburgh Castle lead is unselected and incompatible with a death by 1680 if this weaver identity is right. No 1680 original was newly read: the maintained case has only the supplied wills index, and no linked manuscript or transcription. Neither a marriage nor a mother is supplied. Jonet Kinnie, John’s widow, is not automatically James’s mother. Keep both James profiles separate; they may represent one man, not two proved brothers. The fixed historical cohort and all names, dates, places, spouses, existing father choices and live WikiTree fields are preserved. The circa-1650 birth on James-1376 is an estimate; the newly checked occurrence is in 1672, not a pre-1650 record. One selected uncertain father connects this previously isolated account locally. Supported and confident paternal measurements remain unchanged. Working counts concern retained profile accounts and may include the unresolved duplicate represented by the two James profiles; a gained connection is not another proved person or a proved pedigree. The 27/24 July discrepancy and imprisonment-versus-fine correction remain visible beside the family hypothesis.

It explicitly attaches John Glasgow, born 1745 in Ireland, and Margaret, entered under the surname Nee, as parents. John’s own page cites only Ancestry Family Trees. This verifies what the contributed tree says; it does not verify historical paternity, either parent’s birth, or Margaret’s surname. The page gives Ireland, not County Tyrone. Robert’s more specific Tyrone origin remains an inherited local-profile claim. Select John Glasco of Drumearn (Glasgow-2990) as Robert Glasgow-1189’s possible working father, at 31% subjective confidence. The specific reported father name John favours a John comparison over the automated leading candidate James Glasgow-1970. The actual 1766 Derryloran return places John at Drumearn beside two James Glasco households, three years before Robert’s estimated birth. That supplies a real Tyrone father-generation account compatible with the reported origin. John’s circa-1750 local estimate and the contributed father’s 1745 year are both unproved; either permits fatherhood around 1769, and no date is changed to fit. The estimate assesses the whole proposition that the documented householder was the reported father. It is not a rating of the census record, a statistical probability, or a product of the uncertain ancestry above John. There are two unresolved steps: whether the contributed John/Margaret parentage is correct, and whether that John was the Drumearn householder. A common given name, estimated generation and claimed county cannot establish identity. The 1766 return supplies no wife, child, age or parent; the nearby James entries do not identify John’s father. Robert’s Tyrone birthplace is not independently established by the inspected Geneanet page. John’s existing uncertain James Glasgow-2988 father is preserved, with no new support. The Cookstown reward subscriber of 1796 is an unresolved namesake comparison, with Robert Glasgow-3941 the stronger maintained candidate; that notice supplies no parent and is not used as proof that the Martinsburg man lived at Cookstown. The single Geneanet/Ancestry family-tree chain and its repetition in WikiTree are not independent witnesses. Retain another unidentified Irish John as a serious alternative. John Glasgow-3314, associated with Margaret Mill and the West Calder children of 1762–1770, matches both reported parental given names and a viable generation, but has no inspected Robert or Irish-origin bridge. His Scottish baptism and actual West Calder household are distinct facts; an unproved Irish birthplace is not a categorical exclusion. John Glasgow-4179 of Larne also fits the estimated generation; his known Rose Allan marriage does not prove there was no earlier Margaret, but no record connects him with Robert or Drumearn. James Glasgow-1970 has a Cookstown family tradition and a rare Julia/Julia Ann descendant-name resemblance; those are useful regional clues, but do not outweigh the specific reported John father name. If that report is wrong, James or another local man remains possible. No competing candidate is rejected merely for missing fields. No mother is selected: the reported Margaret is not identified with Margaret Mill, Rose Allan or any existing profile, and Nee is not adopted as a verified birth surname. findings.qualification: The saved biography of John Glasgow-1549 explicitly reports that he and Margaret Hunter sailed for America in 1781 with two young sons, Richard and John (2), and that William was born during the voyage. Its attached children include Richard, William, Matthew and Taylor Wilson, but no John. This is an overlooked, specific family attribution in a contributed account, not a newly discovered passenger list or inspected birth record. The underlying source of the travel and son statements is not identified. The separate will citation must not be presented as having proved those statements: its image could not be inspected in this review. Select John Glasgow of Sinking Valley (Glasgow-1549) as the possible working father of John S. Glasgow Jr. of Cambria (Glasgow-664), at 57% subjective confidence. The family account identifies a missing young son John, while the existing Cambria John supplies a compatible son-generation identity in the same central Pennsylvania settlement area. His reported 1777 Scottish birth would make him about three in 1781, just older than the attached Richard, reportedly born about 1778. The elder John’s estimated 1758 birth permits that generation; neither estimate is a recorded age. The younger man’s Jr. label is modest supporting context, not independent proof of his father’s name. The explicit son report, ordered childhood chronology and regional continuity together favour this particular household over a father chosen only by forename. The 57% assesses both the reliability of the contributed son report and the identification of that son with this later adult; it is not a statistical result or a confidence rating for the whole ancestral path. The freshly inspected 1790 Huntingdon transcription lists John Glasgo, page 116 line 7, with one male aged sixteen or more, five males under sixteen and one female. It gives no names or relationships for the younger people, and does not identify a township for this line. The reported John, Richard, William and Matthew could fit four of those boys, with one unidentified; Taylor Wilson’s reported 1798 birth is later than the return. That is a compatible household comparison, not evidence that those boys were the named sons or that this head was John-1549. Likewise the 1799 Allegheny Township election list may concern the older or younger John or another namesake. The 1820 Cambria locality is supportive regional context, not a continuous personal record from 1790. Keep every census and newspaper identity qualified separately. Another unrecorded son John or a different Scottish immigrant remains possible. John Glasgow-3726, reported born in Cumberland County in 1764 and later in Kentucky, is an older Pennsylvania comparison; his reported birthplace and chronology fit the two young emigrant sons less well, but unverified family dates are not absolute exclusions. John Glasgow-209, reported born in County Londonderry in 1780 and later in Bakerstown, has a different Hugh/Blair parent account and locality history; these are substantive competing family circumstances, rather than proof that every missing John belongs here. The bounded catalogue comparison found no stronger central Pennsylvania John among the checked 1760s–1780s identities. The claimed Daill, Argyll birthplace of John-664 and the Glasgow-city origin in the elder family account remain unverified and are not equated or changed. Glasgow residence of the parents need not identify each child’s birthplace. No mother is selected: Margaret Hunter is the travelling wife in the account, which does not independently establish that she bore this John. No parentage is assigned to Samuel Glasgow-1984 merely because his estimated age could fit the fifth boy. The older Richard Glasgow-1550 attachment and its uncertain Scottish ancestry receive no new support. All existing spouses, children, dates and places remain unchanged; there is no merge, new person or live WikiTree save.

findings.finding: James Glasgow-3523, the Dalziel child of Samuel, is selected as John Glasgow-3094’s possible working father at 41%. The John/Ann Clerk family is recorded in neighbouring Cambusnethan; no record names John’s father.
findings.qualification: John’s saved family association supplies the precise place missing from his broad Scotland birth field: the Ann Clerk marriage is dated 23 October 1790 at Cambusnethan. The maintained child accounts place James Glasgow-3095 there on 11 May 1793 and Samuel Glasgow-3096 there on 17 February 1798, with John named as father in their cited indexes. James Glasgow-3523 represents the Dalziel child indexed 15 March 1719 as son of Samuel Glasgow-3166, under OPR 639,10/28. These are reused family and index citations, not newly inspected register pages; the original entries still need checking. A fresh reading of the printed Dalziel parish account, p. 443, confirms that Cambusnethan bounded Dalziel on the east. That establishes neighbouring parishes, not an individual’s movement or kinship. Select James Glasgow of the 1719 Dalziel record (Glasgow-3523) as John Glasgow-3094’s possible working father, at 41% subjective confidence. This joins the Cambusnethan John-and-Ann family provisionally to the adjacent Dalziel James-and-Samuel family. The positive comparison combines a particular nearby surname household, a viable parent generation, and John’s two currently listed sons James and Samuel repeating the older two given names. Samuel is a more discriminating comparison than John or James alone. The proposed sequence is Samuel to James to John to the later James and Samuel; only the first and last household roles have cited baptismal support. No record names the adult John’s father or shows the 1719 child’s later life. The 41% rates that whole immediate-father proposition, including the child-to-adult identity gap; it is comparative judgment, not a measured frequency or a probability for the complete pedigree. John’s 1770 birth is an uncertain profile estimate, not a baptism or recorded age. If taken literally with 1719 it implies fatherhood at about 51, which is possible and supplies no maternity information. An illustrative John birth in 1750–1770 would give a James age of about 31–51 and a 1790 groom aged 20–40; neither range is adopted as a new date. The 15 March 1719 index date is not independently established as a birthday. The named James may have died young or belonged to another later household. Adjacency does not prove continuity, and an interval of roughly seventy years separates the two parish events. James and Samuel are the currently attached children, not a proved complete or birth-ordered family. Samuel could come from Ann Clerk’s family or another relative; no Scottish naming rule determines the father. The family names and the existing father assignment to Samuel are not independent demonstrations of John’s ancestry. Retain another local James or another unrepresented father, and a collateral relationship to the Dalziel family. Samuel Glasgow-3166 is an alternative direct father if John was substantially older than the 1770 estimate; the ordinary younger-groom generation favours an intervening James, but the absent age cannot exclude an older groom. The earlier Calder Alexander/Clerk-marriage comparison remains a possible wider ancestry route, not a proved direct father: repeated Clerk marriages do not identify Ann’s family or establish a two-century pedigree. Other Scottish James households are not excluded for missing fields, but no comparably specific Cambusnethan–Dalziel and James/Samuel sequence was found in the bounded local catalogue comparison. James’s mother and wife remain unknown. No mother is selected for John, and no relationship is inferred between Ann Clerk and the earlier Clerk women. Preserve the existing ungraded Samuel-to-James father mark and all current child-parent grades, without a confidence upgrade or live save. The 1690s–1794 London pen-cutter comparison for Samuel remains very weak and separate; it supplies no evidence for this family. No person is merged, created or redated.

working_parent_changes.basis: Prefer James Glasgow-991 as the possible working father of the Easter Newtoun adult John Glasgow-3610 at 40% subjective confidence, through the adult’s possible identity with John Glasgow-1084, the Mid Calder child of 1616. working_parent_changes.limitations: The 40% is a combined judgement about James’s fatherhood of the later adult, not the 98% record-defined fatherhood of the 1616 child. The existing 42% childhood-to-adult comparison remains a distinct scoped assessment; these values are not independent measurements and are not mechanically multiplied. Both childhood dates fit an adult father in 1649: about 33 if baptised near birth in 1616, about 41 if in 1608. Neither childhood transcript supplies a residence, occupation or mother. The retained published Edinburgh marriage entry calls the 1642 groom a whipman but supplies no parents or residence to distinguish the candidates. The 1643 child names John and Issobell Porteous; the 1652 Annah transcript names no mother. A household, property, occupation or witness bridge to either childhood is still missing. Another local John, including the retained Linlithgow comparisons, or an unrepresented family remains possible. Robert-4006 remains a father-generation alternative. William-1087 remains a removed unsupported father, not biologically excluded merely by a 1609 baptism. John-1084 and John-3610 may be duplicate accounts, not two proved distinct sons named John; no merge is performed. Mothers remain separately assessed.
